summary: This informational document updates some auxiliary ASN.1 modules for CMS and PKIX from the 1988 syntax to the 2008 one. The old modules stay normative and the wire formats don't change. This helps tools that prefer the newer notation.

plainLanguage.summary: The same data blueprints are rewritten in a newer drawing style. The buildings stay identical, only the blueprint notation changes.

questions: do the cms asn.1 modules change on the wire
which rfcs have updated asn.1 modules in rfc 6268
subtitle: Nine CMS and PKIX data-format modules rewritten in the 2008 ASN.1 notation, with no change on the wire.

tldr.problem: Most security RFCs for PKIX, CMS and S/MIME describe their data formats in the 1988 version of ASN.1, which has been deprecated, and some developers want the latest version used.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6268 republishes nine auxiliary ASN.1 modules in 2008-compliant syntax, built to work with the modules in RFC 5911 and RFC 5912 without importing from anywhere else.
tldr.outcome: The original 1988 modules stay normative and the new ones are informative annexes. The bits on the wire do not change.

today: RFC 6268 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 5911 and has not been obsoleted or updated. The 1988 modules remain the normative definitions.

sections.title: Why Rewrite the Modules
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and many related formats are written down using ASN.1, a notation for describing data structures. Most security RFCs, particularly those about PKIX, CMS and S/MIME, still use the 1988 version of ASN.1, which has been deprecated. Some developers would like the IETF to use the latest version.

This document either converts modules to the 2008 ASN.1 standard or tidies up earlier conversions. It updates RFC 5911 and carries the abstract's key promise: there are no bits-on-the-wire changes to any of the formats. It is only a change to the syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for how secure messages are laid out were written in an old drawing style. This document redraws some of them in the newest style so modern tools can read them.

sections.title: Which Modules Are Covered
sections.content:
The modules come from nine RFCs, each getting its own section:

  • RFC 3274, the compressed data content type for CMS.
  • RFC 3779, X.509 extensions for IP addresses and AS identifiers.
  • RFC 6019, BinaryTime, an alternate date and time format.
  • RFC 4073, protecting multiple contents with CMS.
  • RFC 4231, identifiers and test vectors for HMAC-SHA-224, -256, -384 and -512.
  • RFC 4334, certificate extensions and attributes for authentication in PPP and WLAN.
  • RFC 5083, the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type.
  • RFC 5652, CMS itself.
  • RFC 5752, multiple signatures in CMS.

The text notes that some modules take definitions from different places than the originals did. Combined with the modules in RFC 5911 and RFC 5912, they can stand on their own without importing definitions from anywhere else.
sections.plainLanguage: Nine different rulebooks get the new drawing style. Together with two earlier rewritten books, they cover everything without needing to look anything up elsewhere.

sections.title: What Actually Changed
sections.content:
The 2008 ASN.1 specification adds pre-defined types such as DATE, DATE-TIME, DURATION and TIME-OF-DAY, and the ability to define different encoding rules. None of these newly defined tokens is used in the modules published here.

The more visible edits are in the CMS modules for RFC 5083 and RFC 5652. They define separate attribute sets for the unprotected attributes used in EnvelopedData, EncryptedData and AuthenticatedEnvelopedData, and a parameterized type EncryptedContentInfoType so the same basic type can be used with different algorithm sets. It is assigned to an unparameterized EncryptedContentInfo to keep output changes from earlier versions small.

The point is to let protocol designers constrain attributes by the content type that carries them. Previously attributes could only be constrained by whether they were in the clear or unauthenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: The new style lets designers say which kinds of notes can be stuck on which kinds of envelopes, instead of one rule for every envelope.

sections.title: Normative Status and Module Identifiers
sections.content:
This document does not explicitly update the RFCs the modules were taken from. The original 1988 ASN.1 remains the normative version, and the modules here, like those in RFC 5911 and RFC 5912, are informative annexes.

Section 11 also discusses a way to avoid cascades of edits when a module is replaced: put the module object identifier assignments in one separate module and import them from there. The text is explicit that the modules in this document do not currently implement that idea.
sections.plainLanguage: The old plans are still the official ones. The new drawings are a helpful extra copy, and a handy trick is suggested for keeping the labels easy to change later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document itself has no security considerations. The ASN.1 modules keep the same bits-on-the-wire as the modules they replace, so no protocol behavior changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the messages look exactly the same as before, nothing about how safe they are changes.
